projects.notes: Announced as Meta's largest data center campus; expected to drive significant new electricity demand on Entergy's Louisiana grid. May 9 2026: Meta quietly acquired an additional ~1,400 acres adjacent to the original 2,250-acre Hyperion site for Phase 2 expansion (purchase from George B. Franklin & Sons); cumulative footprint now ~3,650 acres. Entergy's Apr 30 Q1 disclosure attributes ~$15B of its $57B 4-year capital plan to the Meta deal; LPSC-approved order includes $2B in customer-benefit commitments ($140M energy efficiency over 20 years; $60M Power-to-Care bill assistance match). Meta cites $1.6B already contracted with local Louisiana businesses, $1M+ in direct Richland Parish community investment, a $300K contribution to the Richland Revitalization Board, and $215M toward Entergy's customer bill-assistance programs. Grid buildout for the expansion includes 7 new natural-gas generating plants, 3 grid-scale batteries, and potential nuclear development / Waterford 3 expansion, which Entergy projects will save Entergy Louisiana customers more than $2B. Meta VP Rachel Peterson: 'With more than $1.6 billion already contracted with local companies and thousands of jobs being supported, we're delivering real economic impact alongside the AI infrastructure that will power the future.'

Planned 4 buildings; one complete, a second nearly finished, and site work underway on a third as of July 2026. At full build-out will draw at least 160-177 MW peak — about 4x DIA's own peak capacity — making it one of Xcel Energy's largest individual customers (per the original announcement, Colorado Sun, Oct 2023: coloradosun.com/2023/10/11/aurora-data-center-to-become-one-of-xcels-biggest-customers-rivaling-mines-and-steel-mills/). Aurora and Arapahoe County offered tax incentives; the larger draw was a competitive electricity rate, which Colorado PUC staff and the state utility consumer advocate challenged as excessive, recommending a smaller ~15% discount instead. $28M was invested in dedicated high-voltage transmission lines. July 2026 (this record's current source_url): amid reporting that QTS is seeking to expand its on-site diesel backup generator fleet (exact permit figures not independently confirmed — the specific-count source was inaccessible to re-verify directly, so left out here), Aurora councilmember Amy Wiles is pursuing targeted regulations (neighborhood buffers, dropping water-intensive landscaping requirements) rather than a moratorium — 'I personally think we need a neighborhood buffer to make sure they're not being built right next to neighborhoods.' Data centers' diesel generators are subject to Colorado Air Quality Control Commission reporting requirements per the same report. No organized resident opposition group identified in sources reviewed; not enough to source a CommunityResponse record yet.
